name: Akha
confidence_why: Every source read, from Nishida 1966 and Dellinger 1969 to Panadda 1994 and Hayashi 2016, describes Akha as a language with lexical tone on every syllable, and the only disagreement concerns the subordinate word stress, where Hansson 2003's remark that it falls on the highest-toned syllable is outweighed by Nishida 1966 and Panadda 1994, who both place it on the final syllable regardless of tone.

catalog_quote: [Hansson 2003 p.237] There are two phonation types, one breathy, lax (written 'zero'), one laryngealized, tense (written -q). ... There are three tones in open syllables: high -d, mid -a, low (slightly falling) -d, and three in laryngealized syllables: high -dq (very rare), mid -aq, low -dq ... [p.241] The stress in a disyllabic noun is always on the syllable with the highest tone irrespective of whether the syllable is an affix or not. If both syllables have the same tone, the stress is even. phi-ma priest dz@-ma village leader In both words, -ma is a suffix. [Katsura 1973 p.39] The maximum unit treated in this paper is the syllable. The treatment of the relation of one syllable to another, or of linguistic units bigger than the syllable, will be deferred to other occasions. ... [p.43] As the tonemes of Akha, three patterns are observed: I. Mid level type (ML) ... II. Low falling type …
sweep_summary: Both title-works with stress in the title for Akha are unpublished David Bradley manuscripts (1970 'Prosodic phonology of Akha: first approximation', listed by Glottolog as a phonology; 1971 'Prosodies in Akha: questions to investigate'), known only from the SALA bibliography via Glottolog (records saved). No open copy exists in Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, Crossref, archive.org or the STEDT source list; sealang.net was unreachable and WorldCat/HathiTrust/Scholar/Bing blocked or returned noise; Relevance unclear (Firthian prosodic analysis may or may not treat the disyllabic stress alternation); priority medium for the 1970 ms., low for the 1971 agenda note. Re-reading the sources already held by the project yielded two first-hand positional statements: Nishida 1966 p.7 (stress always on the second syllable of a two-syllable sequence, stressed vowel long, tone raised to 55 in that position; Akha shifting to word-pitch accent) and Panadda 1994 pp.21-24 (strong stress on the last syllable of 2-, 3-, 4-syllable words in two Thai Akha dialects, independent of tone). These do not overturn the catalog classification tonal but refine its stress note and conflict with Hansson 2003's highest-tone rule for M-L and H-L tone sequences; Dellinger 1969 uses stress degrees without a placement rule and Katsura 1970 explicitly leaves stress untreated. new_statements.quote: つぎに，2音節連続で前後いずれの位置にたつかによって決定されるアカ語の強勢を中心に，議論を進めたい．さきに述べたごとく，アカ語では，（あとの音節が形態素 -ɯ でない）2音節（2形態素）連続の場合，つねにあとの音節（形態素）に強勢がおかれる．たとえば，［ku11 ʃe:55］〈fish〉：［ʃe11 mɔ:55］〈louse〉 … 前者の形式は，強勢をもって［55］のトーンをとり，後者の形式は，強勢がなく［11］のトーンをとる．… その上，強勢のある音節の母音は，強勢のない音節の母音に比べてつねに長く，二音節連続はあとの音節が〈-ɯ〉でない限り，いつも〔短+長〕の型をとる．このタイプの単語がアカ語にもっとも多い．
new_statements.translation: Next I want to focus the discussion on Akha stress, which is determined by whether a syllable stands first or second in a two-syllable sequence. As stated above, in Akha, in a sequence of two syllables (two morphemes) whose second syllable is not the morpheme -ɯ, stress is always placed on the second syllable (morpheme). E.g. [ku11 ʃe:55] 'fish' : [ʃe11 mɔ:55] 'louse' ... the former form takes stress and tone [55], the latter has no stress and takes tone [11]. ... Moreover the vowel of a stressed syllable is always longer than that of an unstressed syllable, and a two-syllable sequence always takes the [short + long] pattern unless the second syllable is -ɯ. Words of this type are the most numerous in Akha. (Bracketed IPA reconstructed from the garbled text layer; -ɯ = the verb-final bound morpheme.)
new_statements.citation: Nishida, Tatsuo. 1966. Akago no onso taikei [The phonemic system of Akha]. Onsei Kagaku Kenkyu / Studia Phonologica 4: 1-36 (Kyoto University). Japanese with English summary.

new_statements.reading: A first-hand positional rule: within the disyllabic word (the dominant word type) stress is fixed on the FINAL syllable, cued by vowel length, with the stressed syllable taking high tone in the L-H type and the tone of the initial syllable neutralising (numerals 20-900 all become [11 + 55]). Nishida explicitly frames this as a transition from syllable-tone to word-pitch accent. Panadda 1994 (pp.21-24, Thai Akha, two dialects) independently states final strong stress in 2-, 3- and 4-syllable words regardless of tone. Together they refine the catalog's stress note: Hansson 2003's 'stress on the syllable with the highest tone irrespective of [position]' is contradicted for M-L and H-L sequences, where Nishida and Panadda still place stress finally.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the existing Nishida 1966 statement (final syllable of the disyllabic word stressed) and extends it to 3- and 4-syllable words and compounds; the existing statement already cites these pages (pp. 21-24). It fills the catalog's empty rule field with fixed: final syllable. Her tone-independent examples bear against Hansson 2003's 'highest-tone syllable' formulation noted in the existing statement.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Within the phonological word (= stress group) the strong stress is always on the last syllable and every preceding syllable carries weak stress, in 1-, 2-, 3- and 4-syllable words alike; the three compound patterns (p. 24:,w,w 's;,w,w,w 's;,w,w,w 's with reduplication) keep the strong stress on the final syllable of the compound. 4.2.1 defines the major syllable as the one that 'always takes a strong stress' and the minor syllable as taking weak stress. Placement is independent of tone: her examples include strong stress on a low-tone final after a high-tone first syllable, e.g. [ʔa55 'mjoʔ21] 'monkey', [ʔa55 'xoʔ21] 'year', [ʔa55 'phɔ21] 'price' (p. 22).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Not distinguished: all non-final syllables are marked weak (w); no secondary stress grade.
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllables take strong stress only 'usually' (p. 21); no other exceptions. The conclusion (p. 64) states the same four stress-group types hold for both dialects compared (Pa-kha-suk-jai and Lewis's Pu-li).
new_statements.identity_note: Panadda 1994 = Akha of Pa-kha-suk-jai village, Mae Fa Luang, Chiang Rai (Thailand), compared in ch. 6 with Lewis's Pu-li dialect (Burma/Kengtung data); Katsura 1973 = Alu village dialect 55 km NW of Chiang Rai, with the Senchai/Saenchai village dialect 5-10 km away; Hayashi 2018 = Akha Chicho of Ban Pasang, Muang Sing, Luang Namtha, Laos, contrasted with Akha Buli; Nishida 1966 (existing statement) = Thai Akha. All fall under akha1245 (Akha [ahk]); no source treats a variety outside it.

audit.recode_to: Re-settle 'tonal' vs 'fixed-dominant final (final stress)'. If the our rule follows the Pa-O precedent (paok1235: tonal Sino-Tibetan language coded fixed final on a Mahidol 'strong stress on the last syllable of the phonological word' statement), Panadda 1994 ch. III supports fixed-dominant final for Akha; if Hansson 2003's tone-conditioned statement is preferred, keep 'tonal' but add Panadda 1994 pp.21-24 as a 'contra' entry and drop 'No positional.. word-stress rule' from the the primary-stress rule. Also fix the Katsura locator pages to p.38 / p.42.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote check: the deciding Hansson 2003 sentences are verbatim in the held archive.org text layer at the stated pages (237, 241); Katsura portions verbatim modulo scanned spacing but one page off in the locator (38/42 not 39/43). (2) The classification rests on a 2003 16-page survey sketch whose stress remark covers disyllabic nouns only; neither the 271-pp ANU grammar (Dellinger 1969) nor the 124-pp Mahidol phonology (Panadda 1994) in Glottolog's list was. (3) I downloaded six open items (Dellinger 1967, Dellinger 1969, Panadda 1994, Hansson 1989, Lewis 1968 dictionary, Hayashi 2016) into with a record. Five are silent on stress placement and confirm the level-tone system (3 tones, +2 on laryngealized syllables). Panadda 1994 ch. III, however, states an explicit positional rule -- weak-strong with strong stress on the LAST s

Independent first-hand support for Nishida's fixed: final syllable statement; the examples carry tones of every height in the final syllable (e.g. [sa21 da?21] 'salt', [di21 phy21] 'hammer'), so stress is not tied to tone height here, unlike Hansson 2003.

sources.note: Stress is positional, not tone-derived: in any two-syllable (two-morpheme) sequence whose second member is not the bound morpheme -ɯ, stress falls ALWAYS on the second syllable; the stressed vowel is always longer (pattern [short + long]); in the L-H type the unstressed first syllable takes low tone and the stressed second syllable high tone (e.g. [ku11 ʃe:55] 'fish' vs [ʃe11 mɔ:55] 'louse'), and numerals 20-90, 100-900 etc. all neutralise to [short 11 + long 55]. Nishida reads this as Akha shifting from a syllable-tone to a word-tone (word-pitch accent) system. This conflicts with Hansson 20…

sources.quote: 'In Akha, tone is a syllable feature, each syllable having its characteristic pitch and contour' with three tone DFs: high, mid, low; 'The contour of these tones in medial position in an utterance is level ... A low tone on a final syllable always falls.' Stress appears only as SPE-style numerical stress degrees conditioning vowel quality (P5: 'The numbers on the right of the slash mark degrees of stress'; P28 '/e/ ... may be related to a decrease in stress'); no rule placing word stress is given anywhere in the thesis (a full-text search for stress/accent).

sources.quote: 'Oral vowels occur on three level tones: a high tone, a mid tone, a low tone. Laryngealized vowels occur on two level tones: a mid tone, a low tone. The tones of oral vowels tend to be on a level pitch ...' followed by tone-sandhi notes for three low or three high syllables in close juncture and for reduplications. No statement about stress in the introduction (a full-text search for stress/accent pdf pp.1-40: 'stress' absent).

sources.quote: 'The tonemics are based on three pitch levels ... I analyse my informant's speech as having four tones - a low, mid and high level tones, and a falling tone that falls from mid to low pitch' (falling tone utterance-final only); intonation and sandhi 'not investigated thoroughly'. Nothing on stress.

sources.note: Unpublished 1970 manuscript known only from the SALA bibliography entry copied into Glottolog. Title suggests a Firthian-style prosodic (syllable/word-piece) analysis of Akha, which could include the disyllabic stress alternation, but nothing beyond the title is visible. No copy found in Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex, Crossref, archive.org, or the STEDT source list; sealang.net (the SALA host) was unreachable; WorldCat/HathiTrust/Google Scholar blocked automated access.
